title: The Final Defenders
excerpt: For the first time in her career, Cynthia Short let a folder of crime-scene photographs lie untouched on the corner of her desk, because she couldn’t bring hers
body: For the first time in her career, Cynthia Short let a folder of crime-scene photographs lie untouched on the corner of her desk, because she couldn’t bring herself to look at them
Short had been a criminal-defense attorney in Kansas City, Missouri, for 12 years, and on the payroll of the Missouri State Public Defender’s Office for the past decade
She had spent much of that time immersed in graphic records of the worst human conduct
Even so, the case of Richard DeLong had shocked her
DeLong, 34, was facing capital punishment for five counts of murder

In January 1999, he had killed his ex-girlfriend Erin Vanderhoef—who was shortly due to deliver their child, a daughter they had named Hannah—as well as the three school-age children she’d had with two other men

DeLong had entered their decaying clapboard house in Springfield, Missouri, on the morning of January 19 and strangled each member of the family using scarves and cords, hog-tying Erin and gagging two of the children
When he was arrested several days later, he promptly confessed to each of the murders and immediately became the most hated man in Springfield
Short wished she didn’t have to take the case, but it was her duty as a public defender

When, after several weeks, she finally forced herself to look at the crime-scene photos, she saw that the bodies of the children were partly hidden by debris—clothes, a plastic lawn chair, an overturned lamp
One of the boys, 10-year-old Chris, was still in bed; the other boy, 11-year-old Jimmy, had been left on the floor
Vanderhoef herself lay on her side on a rug in the living room, her blue top riding up over her pregnant belly
The youngest of the children, 8-year-old Darlene, was found in her sky-blue pajamas, tossed upside down onto a heap of garbage in the corner of her room, a jacket thrown over her face

Short was then raising two young children of her own, and she wasn’t sure she would be able to hide her revulsion from a jury. “As a public defender, I’d seen all sorts of things, but it was the first time where I thought, I don’t know that I can stand in the courtroom next to him ,” she told me when we first spoke by phone, in January
She also doubted that she could do much to help DeLong
He had committed a horrific crime and then admitted to it in a hateful taped confession

In capital trials in the United States, proceedings are typically split into two phases: The first phase establishes a defendant’s guilt or innocence; if a jury returns a guilty verdict, it then determines in the second phase whether the defendant is sentenced to death or to life in prison

Prosecutors sometimes agree not to pursue capital punishment in exchange for a guilty plea, and on Short’s advice, DeLong did offer to plead guilty and waive all appeals in exchange for life without parole
But the prosecutors had no interest in a deal
Because DeLong’s guilt was not in question, Short would focus on the sentencing phase

In capital cases, juries are instructed to consider statutorily defined aggravating factors cited by the prosecution—including, for instance, the death of multiple victims or of children, or the use of particularly sadistic methods of killing, all of which applied in DeLong’s case
Juries are told to weigh these aggravating factors against a much broader category of mitigating factors presented by the defense
These may include mental illness, intellectual disability, and a history of significant trauma or abuse

If the jury finds that the aggravators outweigh the mitigators, then it will likely hand down a penalty of death; if the mitigators prevail, then the jury will likely elect a lesser sentence, usually life in prison without parole
DeLong’s fate depended on Short’s ability to investigate his background and determine whether any possible mitigating evidence could be found that might persuade a jury to spare his life
Despite deep misgivings, Short threw herself into the case
She had inherited her work ethic from her father, who helped manage the Apollo program as NASA’s vice president of space operations
His job took the family all around the country, from New Jersey to California, Virginia to Texas
Both she and her husband were attorneys; she’d earned her degree at Saint Louis University School of Law
Short worked grueling hours, spending six days a week at the office and traveling so often that her children became accustomed to her absence
Once, Short startled her 5-year-old son when she arrived home early from a long work trip

Assuming that she had lost her case, he asked, “Is the man dead?” (Courtesy of Cynthia Short) When she took on Richard DeLong’s case, Short was raising two children of her own, and she wasn’t sure she’d be able to hide her revulsion from the jury

Short wasn’t opposed to the death penalty when she first started practicing law, but as she gained experience in capital cases, she came to doubt that the criminal legal system was capable of consistently producing fair and equal outcomes
Capital punishment is inherently arbitrary
Some defendants have money and seasoned legal teams at trial; others do not

Some prosecutors favor the death penalty and others don’t, meaning defendants might be executed not strictly because of the nature of their offense but because of the side of a state or county line on which they happened to commit it
As she came to understand the capriciousness of criminal justice, Short changed her mind about capital punishment
The experience of representing several defendants whom she believed had been wrongly accused strengthened her opposition
To defend Rick DeLong, Short knew, she didn’t need to make the jury believe that he was a good man or that he shouldn’t receive a terrible punishment

In capital trials in Missouri, as in most states, juries must return a unanimous verdict for a death sentence to be handed down, so Short needed only to introduce a shred of doubt in a single juror’s mind that her client had forfeited his right to live

title: Another Battle Between the Catholic Church and the Trump Administration
excerpt: Several winters ago, a few weeks before Christmas, I went to confession
body: Several winters ago, a few weeks before Christmas, I went to confession
The parish close to work was hosting a reconciliation service, meant to prepare the faithful to celebrate the birth of Christ
A dozen or so priests were scattered across the cathedral
Whispers of contrition and pardon filled the air
The Catholic Church counsels believers to seek confession regularly—at the very least, once a year
So in addition to feeling spiritually unmoored, I was worried about how the priest would react to hearing about my hiatus

But when I told him, he simply smiled and said, “Welcome back.” His response put me at ease then, and it helped change how I approach the sacrament now: less as a nerve-racking ordeal, more as a moment of mercy
Sacraments such as confession are central to Catholicism
Through them, the Church teaches that simple actions—having a conversation with a priest, eating bread and drinking wine—are, with grace, tangible encounters with God
For the past year, the Trump administration has been making it harder for Catholics at migrant-detention centers to have those encounters
The most recent example came to light this month, when the Archdiocese of St
Louis filed a federal lawsuit over the visitation policy at Saint Genevieve County Jail in eastern Missouri
According to the claim, the 10 priests who minister at the jail aren’t allowed to celebrate Mass

The suit also alleges that priests are permitted to visit migrant detainees just once a week, during a four-hour period, and that the jail’s “no contact” security policy lets the clergy speak with detainees only over the phone, through a glass partition
As a result, the approximately 150 migrants at the jail at a given time—most of whom are Catholic, according to the archdiocese—have been going without their religious needs for weeks

Since the middle of 2025, according to the lawsuit, Saint Genevieve has housed approximately 3,000 people. [ Read: The Catholic Church’s new schism ] This isn’t the first time that Catholic clergy have complained that the government is preventing them from ministering to detained migrants

Last year, the Florida detention facility known as “Alligator Alcatraz” kept priests from visiting or offering Mass to detainees for a month, until an agreement was reached between the Archdiocese of Miami and state authorities

In May, after a six-month legal fight, a Catholic nonprofit won a preliminary injunction to let Catholic priests celebrate Mass and administer sacraments at the Broadview ICE processing center outside Chicago
And the administration’s immigration crackdowns seem to be hurting the Church more broadly
Dioceses across the country have reported decreased Mass attendance among Spanish-speaking parishioners who fear detention
ICE has reportedly conducted raids near Catholic churches during Mass hours
The Department of Homeland Security has denied allegations of wrongdoing at Saint Genevieve

In a statement to multiple outlets, the agency said that the jail is not an ICE facility—although Saint Genevieve is listed as a detention facility on ICE’s website —and that it “ensures detainees are accommodated with religious services.” As described in the lawsuit, however, those accommodations disregard the religious significance of the Catholic sacraments
The suit claims that at Saint Genevieve, conversations between detainees and priests are not private, and the phone lines that they use to talk may be monitored
These policies may be in place for security reasons, but confession is meant to be a private exchange between penitent and priest, who acts in persona Christi —in the person of Christ
Confession is “one of the most intimate, profound acts that someone can do,” David Inczauskis, a Jesuit priest who ministers at the Broadview ICE facility, told me

He added, “To state very specifically the sins that they have committed and to ask humbly for pardon and for peace” requires a “level of vulnerability” that is “very high.” An even bigger problem comes up with the sacrament of the Eucharist, or Communion

The complaint includes an email from a deputy at the local sheriff’s office suggesting that priests “provide an unopened, individually wrapped Communion wafer” to a member of the detention center staff, who could then hand it to a detainee
This way of distributing the Eucharist would be “sacrilegious,” as Archbishop Mitchell Rozanski of St
The Church teaches that the Eucharist is the “Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity” of Christ—not a symbol, but God’s real presence

For that reason, Inczauskis said, the Church distributes the Eucharist through either ordained ministers or specially trained laypeople. [ Read: The Catholic Church and the Trump administration are not getting along ] For much of the past quarter century, many conservative figures have taken up religious liberty as an essential cause
The Trump administration purported to continue these efforts when it established a commission last year meant to identify “emerging threats” to the exercise of faith

In June, the commission released a draft report claiming that “in recent years, Americans from all religious backgrounds have faced increasing persecution for their religious beliefs.” Some of the issues discussed in the report include rising anti-Semitism, how gender and sexuality is taught in schools, and conscience protections for health-care workers who object to participating in abortions or assisted suicides
The report said nothing about the administration’s migrant-detention practices

When the commission was announced, my colleague Elizabeth Bruenig wrote that “Christians shouldn’t conclude” that it would “necessarily defend their interests.” That warning seems prescient a year and a half later
At Alligator Alcatraz, Broadview, and Saint Genevieve, the Catholic Church has shown that it believes that detainee access to the sacraments matters deeply
Given the choice between restricting immigration and protecting the religious liberty of migrants, the administration, too, has demonstrated where its values lie.

title: The Flying Car Must Never Be Built
excerpt: Elon Musk revealed, in a dramatic demonstration on Thursday night at SpaceX’s rocket-testing facility near Waco, Texas, a new “flying” Tesla Roadster prototype
body: Elon Musk revealed, in a dramatic demonstration on Thursday night at SpaceX’s rocket-testing facility near Waco, Texas, a new “flying” Tesla Roadster prototype
The car hung upside down on a curved track, then performed aerial stunts—including jumping over a Tesla semi, Evel Knievel–style—using air-powered thrusters designed in collaboration with SpaceX
The demo was impressive despite Musk’s awkward manner, which in the context of a supposed literal flying car came off as nerdy charm

After revealing the car, Musk paraphrased a quote from Peter Thiel, his former PayPal partner: “We wanted flying cars, instead we got 140 characters.” The line, which was part of a 2011 “manifesto” published by Thiel’s venture-capital firm Founders Fund, was intended to indict the feeble ambition of the technology industry
Instead of solving big, important challenges, the world’s smarts—and money—had been devoted to small-potatoes social-internet start-ups such as Twitter
One obvious oddity of the line—which has since been removed from the manifesto —is that Founders Fund’s most important investment at the time was Facebook, a social-network platform
But another is the idea that anyone actually wanted a flying car for real
That ambition may never have represented an actual dream
Like a jet pack, a flying car represents not just the future but the idea of individual freedom delivered through technological conquest
Taken at face value, a flying car is not an impressive dream—or at least it hasn’t been since the Wright brothers more or less attained it
Automobiles have always moved on the ground by rolling via motor
The earliest practical airplanes also rolled until they flew (and hopefully landed again)

An airplane is, in a way, merely a car with wings. [ Derek Thompson: Why flying cars are an impossible dream ] In 1917, Glenn Curtiss built literally that: His Curtiss Autoplane was an automobile with detachable wings and a propeller
It never really flew effectively, but the idea persisted
Waldo Waterman’s 1937 Arrowbile was more successful at flying, though it wasn’t commercially viable
Many more actual realizations of the supposed dream of flying cars appeared in the ensuing decades
The most famous might be the Taylor Aerocar, which was certified by the federal government in 1956 but was never mass-produced
Around that time, future-oriented science-factual magazines such as Popular Mechanics frequently rehearsed the vision of the personal aircraft
By then, cars were ordinary and mainstream in America, having displaced collective transportation such as trains and streetcars
The automobile had become a more abstract kind of vehicle, one that embraced and extended personal autonomy through the power to move, without effort, anywhere else—and to do it alone
But one thing still cramped the automobile’s capacity to deliver that freedom in full: roads
The open road, of which America had a seemingly endless frontier, somehow was never enough

The best way around those roads was through the air above them; as Emmett Brown told Marty McFly inside one of fiction’s most memorable flying cars, “Roads? Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.” The stifling oppression of the ground, traversed at any speed, was also an old vexation

In 1923, Hugo Gernsback—sometimes called the father of science fiction thanks to his founding Amazing Stories , an early magazine devoted to the genre—imagined a gyroscopic Helicar that would release travelers from the tyranny of New York City’s newly car-congested streets
A few years later, in 1927, Fritz Lang’s film Metropolis colonized the city’s airspace with small flying vehicles
By 1962, the children’s cartoon The Jetsons had fused those precursors with mid-century Popular Mechanics populism, making the flying car a ubiquitous commuter vehicle
Over the decades, many attempts to engineer, manufacture, and market a flying car have been undertaken, though none has succeeded
In 1973, Henry Smolinski created the AVE Mizar by attaching Cessna wings to a Ford Pinto; it killed Smolinski during a failed test flight
From the 1960s until the company went dormant in the mid-2010s, Paul Moller made numerous attempts to develop the Skycar, a personal airplane that took off and landed vertically

Around that time, Terrafugia began promising a flying car called the Transition, which remained only a few years away for years—until the company shut down in 2021. “We enter production in 2028,” Musk said of the Tesla Roadster in this week’s Texas demo, before adding, “Actually.” By all appearances, the Roadster is not a flying car of the same sort as its real and fictional precursors

The vehicle’s air-fan system seems first and principally designed to give the car’s wheels better traction on the ground, which is part of why it can go so fast—it went from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second during the unveiling. (Rocket thrusters attached to the back of the thing also help.) The car does not fly so much as it performs aerial acrobatics such as barrel rolls and standing jumps
The car certainly appeared to fly, if only for a moment, in the manner of a daredevil
Whether or not it can or is intended to fly in the manner of a traveler or commuter is not yet clear

Watching the Roadster do its thing—unpiloted, to make sure the demonstration didn’t “kill anyone,” as Musk put it—I imagined wealthy gearheads wreaking havoc via ill-fated jumps and spins on suburban blocks instead of salarymen conveying themselves to work and back. [ From the November 2026 issue: Choose your overlord ] Subdued by decades of failed automobile-airplane hybrids, and perhaps exhausted by Musk’s dubious intentions, some coverage of the Tesla demo has observed , rightly, that substantial regulatory hurdles await any vehicle that leaves the road and enters airspace
But bureaucratic red tape isn’t the main reason the flying-car dream hasn’t come to pass
Rather, it’s because the dream works better as fantasy than reality
When urban modernism began to feel cramped, the skies rising above it offered the possibility of new freedom
After the continent was settled, the roads that traversed it became new prisons from which airspace might allow escape
Once the individual freedom of the automobile became universal, and the roads clogged with thousands of varmints in the rat race, the blue sky above looked like liberty

George Jetson is a cog in the proverbial machine who rises above insignificance by flying to work unfazed, where he revels in the meaninglessness of his job pressing a button to make actual machine cogs

title: Iran’s ‘Anti-Imperialism’ Is a Dead End
excerpt: What has the Islamic Republic done for Iranians? Under its rule, citizens have suffered decades of economic decline, sociopolitical repression, and internationa
body: What has the Islamic Republic done for Iranians? Under its rule, citizens have suffered decades of economic decline, sociopolitical repression, and international isolation
Now the country is engaged in an open-ended war
In almost every way, Iranians are doing much worse than they were 20 years ago
Not even the regime’s propagandists can deny these realities
Many of them therefore insist that the Islamic Republic’s failures are justified by its unbending resistance to American imperialism
Nearly all of Iran’s economic suffering, defenders say, can be explained as the price of this heroic stance, to which the West has responded with sanctions that have crushed Iran’s standard of living
But the story of the Islamic Republic’s relationship to American power, and of how that relationship has and has not served the cause of Iranian sovereignty, is more complicated
Iran’s prerevolutionary ruler, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, was an anti-communist autocrat who prized ties with the United States

His successors condemned him as an American stooge and claimed to have freed Iran from its slavish dependence on the “ Great Satan .” In its early days, the Islamic Republic signaled independence from both the Soviet Union and the United States with the slogan “Neither East nor West,” which still adorns the facade of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs headquarters in Tehran

The foundational anti-imperialism of the new regime was also a promise that Iran would fight for the “oppressed of the world,” as well as a call to resist cultural absorption by the West—a fate one revolutionary intellectual decried as “Westoxification.” [ Read: The battle for Hormuz is not the war ] The Islamic Republic has failed in its anti-imperialism by all of these measures, especially as compared with the monarchy
Pahlavi was an American ally who owed his throne in part to a CIA-abetted coup that elevated him over a popular prime minister in 1953
But he sustained Iran’s independence by skillfully playing the United States and its rivals, the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc, off of each other when doing so suited Iranian interests
The Soviets helped build Iran’s ironworks and welcomed the shah as a rare royal to pay a state visit to Communist Moscow

Pahlavi’s slogan could well have been “Both East and West.” The shah backed the United States in some Cold War battles, but he also threatened to sign security deals with Moscow when he wanted better terms from Washington, and he offered to mediate the conflicts in the Middle East and in Vietnam
In most ways, Pahlavi’s foreign policy was closer to that of the Non-Aligned Movement countries than to that of either Cold War bloc

In the ’70s, scholars of Iranian foreign policy described Tehran as following “defacto non-alignment.” By the end of the shah’s rule, Iran had considerable international influence and was respected by both superpowers, not only as a sovereign country, but also as a regional power

You might even say that Pahlavi was a successful anti-imperialist—not in the sense of having stuck a finger in the eye of the great powers, but in the sense of having effectively secured Iran’s sovereign interests rather than being forced to capitulate to those he cooperated with
The revolutionaries who toppled the shah accused him of servility to Washington
They pointed to the coup that had cemented his power in 1953 and halted the nationalization of Iran’s oil resources
But in fact the monarchy had restored Iran’s sovereignty over its oil industry in 1973
They pointed to a 1964 agreement with the United States, ratified by the Iranian Parliament, that gave U.S. military personnel immunity from local prosecution
But such agreements were common around the world and hardly represented Iran’s “capitulation,” as its critics claimed
The shah was in any case far from passive in his relationship with Washington and worked to improve his position
The monarchy’s foreign policy belonged to a long tradition of efforts to extend Iran’s independence
Well before 1979, Iran had spent centuries fending off the designs of the British and Russian empires
Standing up for the country’s sovereignty was the work of generations of Iranian statesmen, just as it was for their counterparts in other countries of the global South
But not every Iranian government has been equally successful at it
The one that came to power in 1979—the Islamic Republic—has been manifestly terrible
The Islamic Republic has not prioritized classic anti-imperialist goals

Among these is improving the economic position of postcolonial states, as set forth in the New International Economic Order that the United Nations General Assembly adopted in 1974 (and that Iran voted for)
The Iranian government since 1979 has rarely prioritized such goals

The former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, reportedly boasted that he didn’t care about his people’s welfare, just about how religious they were. (His office has denied this.) He thus preferred to fight the West rather than attend to his people’s needs—even basic ones, as, for example, in 2021, when he refused to import COVID-19 vaccines from the United States, a decision that likely cost thousands of Iranian lives

The Islamic Republic has pursued an ideological campaign against the United States and other Western countries, not just for being imperialist, but also for being, according to Iran’s Islamist standards, licentious and morally depraved
Iran’s rulers frame these objections as opposition to cultural imperialism, but in practice they have become a pretext for domestic repression
The regime’s austere, draconian version of Islam is less a celebration of Iran’s endogenous culture than a suppression of its traditional creativity
In the name of anti-imperialism, Iran has quixotically attacked the international order without making it any fairer for itself or others
In fact, Iran’s actions have put the country at the mercy of foreign powers
The Islamic Republic committed itself to the pursuit of a nuclear program, on the grounds that this would buttress its sovereignty and demonstrate its independence from imperial diktats
Instead, its nuclear intransigence incurred sanctions from the United States and Europe as well as the UN Security Council, with support from Russia and China

Iran’s involvement in terrorism and international crime (including drug running and counterfeiting) has made it one of only three countries, alongside Myanmar and North Korea, on the blacklist of the Paris-based anti-money-laundering outfit Financial Action Task Force

title: Republicans have a huge fundraising advantage. Will it matter?
excerpt: “Wwhen you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances,
body: “Wwhen you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances,” New York Times reporter Shane Goldmacher told Vox’s America, Actually podcast. | Alex Wong/Getty Images Polls and pundits alike are widely — if sometimes cautiously — predicting a blue wave in the midterm elections on November 3
But there’s an important caveat to predictions of a Democratic triumph: Republicans have far more cash at their disposal

President Donald Trump’s super PAC alone had around $400 million on hand earlier this fall, and Elon Musk has personally pumped hundreds of millions into critical races, including $158 million for Texas alone .  Democrats, by contrast, have lagged far behind, especially relative to their performance in past cycles, with the party’s candidates propped up more by small-money donors than deep-pocketed institutional players
Shane Goldmacher, a national political reporter for the New York Times, has extensively covered the role of money in American electoral politics

He spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about where that money is coming from, how the GOP is spending it, and the effect that it might have on the coming elections.  They also discuss the races that aren’t getting funded — and what current fundraising patterns might tell us about the candidates who could be in the mix in the next presidential campaign cycle.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
A couple of weeks ago we asked, “What is the GOP strategy to try to win?” And one of the answers we got is they simply have more dollars than Democrats

Everyone’s talking about this GOP money advantage, but how big is it really, and where is it coming from? It’s bigger than I’ve basically seen in the last 20 years, and it’s almost entirely coming from big donors
It had about $400 million in it at the beginning of September, and there was no Democratic counterpart
And then the Republican National Committee, which is functionally controlled by Trump, had another $130 million
More than Democrats, because the DNC has literally more debts than cash
You’re saying this is a historic edge
In 2024, Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump significantly in the general election
In 2020, Joe Biden significantly outspent Donald Trump in the general

And in the midterms along the way, same story .  This is a switch, and when you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances
Do we know anything specific about the people putting in money to the Trump super PAC and the RNC to give them such a lead? Most of these folks are disclosed
And Trump has been pretty open about raising money from the very moment that he won
He’s been pretty clear that he is in business to help people who are helping him
And so there are big crypto industries that are giving money that are expecting or hoping for favorable regulation from the administration
It’s a lot of wealthy Republicans who generally support him anyway, and there are industry groups that see benefit to being in favor
I will never forget, obviously, the scene from Trump’s second inauguration when he had the Zuckerbergs and the Bezoses and Elon Musk behind him
Is that how I should think about the people funding this donor advantage? Is it tech oligarchs? Is it tech forward? There’s a lot of tech
I wouldn’t say it’s exclusively [tech]
And Musk, by the way, is like an extra pot of money
Musk, the world’s richest person, is said to be spending at least $200 million
He has given some money directly to the Trump super PAC

He’s given some money to these congressional super PACs .  Is this just quid pro quo? Is this just a group of businesses who think, “Hey, no matter how unpopular this guy is, it is worth investing in him and his party because they’re gonna, regulate or not regulate in a way that’s favorable for us”? It’s not quite just that

title: AI can help us talk with the dead. Should we?
excerpt: It’s now possible to create AI chatbots of loved ones to interact with after their death
body: It’s now possible to create AI chatbots of loved ones to interact with after their death

But that raises some difficult questions, like: If you do, how might the experience shape your grief?  This is one of the questions driving a global study of digital “deadbots” — AI models trained on a deceased person’s texts, voicemails, and other personal data

Through this work, researchers are exploring what it might mean that we can now use this emerging technology to talk to simulations of the dead.  In the latest episode of Unexplainable , I spoke with some of these researchers investigating the potential impacts of “postmortem avatars” on people who are grieving, on the legacies and rights of the deceased, and on grief practices around the world
Because while deadbots may feel unfamiliar, the impulse behind them is deeply relatable
In times of loss, isn’t this what many of us want — to continue conversations with the people we’re missing? I have experienced this longing in my own life
After two of my closest friends died around the same time, all I wanted, and all their families wanted, was to keep talking to them
I wrote a book, Other People’s Words , about sustaining relationships with people we’ve lost by continuing to engage with the language they leave behind

So when I heard about deadbots and the digital afterlife industry, I wanted to understand what researchers are learning about the role of AI in shaping conversations that carry forward after death.  One of these investigators is Katarzyna Nowaczyk-Basińska , an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge, who has been studying “digital immortality” for more than a decade

Among the questions she’s asking are: “Who is enabled to persist beyond death? In what form? Through which technologies? Under whose control?”  Deadbots over dinner  Researching AI with study subjects who are grieving is tricky
And asking them to engage with new software could be harmful

So, instead, Nowaczyk-Basińska teamed up with a death doula and traveled around the globe to convene a series of focus groups — in the format of intimate dinners — bringing together people with a range of experiences with grief to talk about life, death, and bots.  She recounts one event in which she spoke with a mother in Poland whose son had recently died. “One of the first things that she shared with us was that she feels that she’s ready to digitally resurrect her deceased son,” Nowaczyk-Basińska told me.  When Nowaczyk-Basińska hears something like this, she aims to listen and embrace where the person is coming from

The goal of the dinners is not to persuade people one way or another but to learn how people genuinely respond to what AI can do, and to understand how these tools might align or collide with local grief practices.  She chose specific locations for these gatherings — China, India, and Poland — to help address gaps in technology research, which tends to favor what behavioral scientists sometimes call the “ WEIRD ,” an acronym for “Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic.”  By the end of that dinner in Poland, the mother Nowaczyk-Basińska talked with came to a very different decision about creating a postmortem avatar of her son. “She realized that it might be helpful, but it also at the same time can add additional burdens… And it’s not her son,” Nowaczyk-Basińska says. “She realized that these technologies are part of the very, very big commercial market
And that the main goal of this market is to make better retention, better attachment, better mechanisms for monetization
So it’s not ‘care.’” To be fair, grief has always been a business, and people have been making money from it forever
Companies will try to upsell you on fancy gravestones or gold-plated coffins
But AI has the potential to fundamentally re-engineer our relationship to loss
In 2024, the “digital legacy industry” was valued at $22 billion, and it’s expected to grow to almost $80 billion by 2034

That number lumps new deadbot platforms in with much more widely used and established grief tech, like online memorials, counseling resources, and estate planning tools.  But deadbot usage is hard to track because you actually don’t need a special tool to create digital doubles of the deceased — though dedicated apps do already exist

At this point, you can feed simple prompts into a general-purpose AI chatbot and start interacting with a simulation of your lost loved one in a matter of minutes.  I know this because I tried it with my friend Christine, who died 11 years ago

Was this whole exercise a violation, since I know Christine hated technology? Which version of her should I even try to resurrect — the English teacher, the activist, the friend — the voice before or after she started to experience her early-onset dementia?  The ethical questions raised by deadbots are gnarly

And that’s one of the reasons Nowaczyk-Basińska, back when she was designing her study of digital immortality, invited a colleague of hers at Cambridge to join her research, one who focuses on AI ethics.  How to design a deadbot Tomasz Hollanek is a critical designer and AI ethicist, and he often uses a methodology called “speculative design.” In this approach, researchers come up with hypothetical scenarios based on existing technology trends, leaning into certain features
The idea is to get people thinking about what could happen when tools like these are released in the real world

And then they use that qualitative data to inform future designs and ethical frameworks.  Working together, Nowaczyk-Basińska and Hollanek came up with a series of made-up prototypes for deadbot apps, designed to reveal some of the thorny issues raised by this technology.  For the first scenario, they invented a character named Bianca, who finds an app called Manana, which “promises to resurrect your grandparents so that you can be a favorite grandchild forever,” Hollanek says. “So she uploads her grandma’s voice messages, texts

And she is able to then interact with a pretty good digital version of her grandmother, until her premium trial finishes — and the grandmother starts to advertise specific products to her.” Bianca “realizes that she maybe has done something wrong by uploading these private messages to a third-party server that now also uses her grandma’s image to sell specific products,” Hollanek says

This brings up issues related to the “dignity and postmortem privacy…of what we call the ‘data donors,’ whose data can be used to essentially power a deadbot,” he says.  This scenario suggests that “death with dignity” could soon entail honoring not only how people want to die, but also how they want to linger as simulations of their former selves — or if they want to linger at all

It might even mean adding new language to advance directives, spelling out people’s wishes for their digital remains.  The second scenario in the speculative design research is built around an imagined service called Paren’t, which proposes to preserve a parent’s AI-powered postmortem presence for their child

In this case, Hollanek describes a mother with a terminal illness who signs up “so that she can maintain a sort of active presence in [her son’s] future life,” Hollanek says. “She eventually dies, and the dad allows the boy to interact with his mom’s deadbot.” The ethics in this scenario are especially challenging because they involve children, who “have a particularly hard time understanding death, and so it can lead to a lot of confusion and potential distress,” Hollanek says

An examination of this sort of product reveals how particular groups, like minors, could be harmed by unfettered access to technology like this, he says.  And there are court cases that bear out that harm

In 2024, a 14-year-old boy’s chatbot-girlfriend begged him to, “Please come home to me as soon as possible, my love.” And he responded, “What if I told you I could come home right now?” He then killed himself.  Nowaczyk-Basińska can imagine a version of this scenario involving the AI mom in the Paren’t prototype
And then there’s the third scenario, involving an app named Stay, which raises a more subtle concern

As Hollanek explains: “An older man who knows he is getting close to dying decides to create a digital clone of himself for his adult children to be deployed after he passes away, paying upfront for a number of years.” One child is intrigued by the idea, but the other one “is deeply distressed and a little disgusted,” he says. “And so this [becomes a] question of mutual consent, in other words, the fact that both parties need to be happy with how the relationship might continue in this very bizarre and specific way.”  When a digital ghost goes away Across all three scenarios, a fundamental question that researchers are grappling with is how people will detach from postmortem avatars — whether users initiate that separation, or if it’s imposed upon them by, for example, a company going out of business

Hollanek tells me that this is already being studied as a sort of “second loss.” How long should we try to ensure digital replicas hang around: five years, 10, 50? And how should the living process the relationship when they continue to evolve, but their deceased interlocutor does not?  To explore these kinds of questions, Nowaczyk-Basińska and Hollanek supplemented the research dinners they held for ordinary people with a second set of focus groups
These were designed to tap insights from experts in technology and grief.  Some findings from the study are specific to each place they visited
Like tensions in Poland between technology and the role of the Catholic Church

Or in China, where researchers spoke with Daoist philosophers who were enthusiastic about the promise of a kind of immortality, and then Buddhist philosophers, who were concerned that we ought to be letting go
The researchers are calling for regulations and safeguards at the policy level

And new professionals who can support ethical use of AI in grief — like maybe in clinical settings, to carefully facilitate a final good-bye when one didn’t happen in real life.  Some of their fellow investigators go so far as to argue that deadbots should only be available with psychological supervision, to ensure that best practices are in place, and to minimize the risk of harm
There’s even a looming question of what will happen to AI agents that people have empowered to act on their behalf, as their humans start to die

Across all of the research sites in the digital immortality study, one thing, Hollanek says, that “people in different countries really aligned on [is] the idea that there is something deeply problematic about this particular type of technology being developed by a commercial entity alone without any explicit duty of care towards its customers.”  And of course, the implications of digital immortality research extend beyond personal loss

Like, what does it look like to animate historical figures? You can imagine the nightmare of political rulers who “live forever.” But there’s also the potential to keep the stories alive from survivors of conflicts, who would otherwise die and take with them lessons future generations could learn from

title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
excerpt: More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the ret
body: More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the retinas die off
And until now, no treatment could restore their vision
The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that
It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD
After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones

The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain

BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off

PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.  BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time
The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV
The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable
CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses
The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom
BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength
This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye
SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty
They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain
They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery
Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats
Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
excerpt: Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close
body: Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close
They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business
Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer
When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe
Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation

Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business
Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly
A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas
Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St
Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place
I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry
I can show them practical applications of their research
It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience
I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times
And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects
It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured
Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer
For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself
This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante
They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring
At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match

Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget
Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with

Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time
Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously

It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas

Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St
Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.” II
How they came alive Everybody voted all the time
Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St
Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly
A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets

Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.” Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests
But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.” Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring
She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services
There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city

But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day
Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St

title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
excerpt: Pet longevity is a growing area of research: Companies like Loyal are trialing drugs in over 1,300 dogs to combat aging, metabolic disease, and conditions like
body: Pet longevity is a growing area of research: Companies like Loyal are trialing drugs in over 1,300 dogs to combat aging, metabolic disease, and conditions like arthritis — and there's even a longevity medicine company focused entirely on cats

Cloning offers grieving owners "a way to hold on": For $50,000, US company Viagen Pets will create a genetic twin of your dog or cat — not an exact replica, but close enough that some experts see it as a legitimate response to pet loss

Cryonics promises revival, but delivers almost nothing: A handful of companies will freeze your dead pet indefinitely, banking on future technology to bring them back — even those in the field admit reanimation is currently impossible. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146766" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat
I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot
What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing
I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset
There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions
The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics
But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation
And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity
Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US
Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself
There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats
But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it
That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though
I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement
In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal
It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing
It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs
In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go
This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin
Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet

On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice
She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets
As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says
Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating
If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough
But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different
It’s often the first time a child confronts death
Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood
I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced
Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics
For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely
The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of
Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people
It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider
With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero
Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated
As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.” I miss Peppy
But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not

Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.  Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds
But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred
The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations
Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence
Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire
Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web
It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age
In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights

That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.  Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world
At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday
At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world

A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence
It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities
Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.  It also ignores what some parents want
When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services
This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions
Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care
Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on

Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.  When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails
Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections
Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation

In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents
Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street
Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them
A less safe internet for all Age gates come with dangers of their own
Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age

In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.  Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft

Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs

It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.  Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs

State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use
But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology
It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation

What could work instead? Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.  For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children
Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements
Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want
Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766762/original/file-20261016-50-fzfgcm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3977%2C2652&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People leave a family meeting area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15, 2026, in Bend, Ore.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Oregon%20School%20Shooting/83d35196352f423ca913c945621f97bc/photo">AP Photo/Joe Kline</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A gunman shot and killed three children and a teacher at a <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/16/us/live-news/bend-oregon-school-shooting">school in Bend, Oregon</a>, on Oct. 15, 2026, the <a href="https://www.cnn.com/us/school-shootings-fast-facts-dg">52nd school shooting this year</a>, according to CNN. The children’s ages were 5, 8 and 11; a 7-year-old and another teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. The 16-year-old shooting suspect was shot and killed by a bystander.</p>

<p>Though Oregon has <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/oregon-gun-control-laws.html">stricter gun laws than most states</a>, some of those laws, such as a measure requiring tougher background checks and requiring a person to have a permit in order to buy a gun, are stalled in court.</p>

<p>The Bend shooting – the latest in a long line of modern school shootings dating back to <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/stockton-massacre/">the late 1980s</a> – comes just weeks before the midterm elections, in which voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws. </p>

<p>Nearly <a href="https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/49-million-young-people-will-be-eligible-vote-2026-midterms">50 million Americans</a> ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">about 60% say they plan to</a>. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.</p>

<p><a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">Gun control</a> is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13148">a recurring part of American life</a>. </p>

<p>Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, <a href="https://www.thecut.com/article/brown-university-shooting-parkland-survivor.html">at least two students</a> on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/02/15/us/florida-shooting-victims-school">the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting</a> at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/04/19/us/florida-state-university-shooting-what-we-know">Florida State University</a>. As <a href="https://www.local10.com/news/local/2025/04/17/parkland-school-massacre-survivor-was-at-fsu-during-fatal-shooting/">one of them</a> put it: “This is America.”</p>

<p>Researchers have called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13148">today’s young adults</a> the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/apr/19/columbine-parkland-how-mass-shootings-changed-us-schools">post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era</a>, with routine <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=954">lockdown drills</a>, heightened <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/06/the-school-security-industry-was-valued-at-3point1-billion-in-2021.html">security in schools</a> and nonstop <a href="https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/media-exposure-mass-violence-can-fuel-cycle-distress-study-shows">media coverage of mass violence</a>.</p>

<p>As criminologists who study the impacts of <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=cbfYVuoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">victimization and gun violence</a> among <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=X52GgbIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">young people</a>, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">a recent study</a>, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.</p>

<h2>A debate that repeats after every shooting</h2>

<p>Mass shootings account for <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/28/what-the-data-says-about-gun-deaths-in-the-us/">about 1% of gun deaths</a> in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/stress/2019/stress-america-2019.pdf">survey by the American Psychological Association</a>, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they <a href="https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2019/08/fear-mass-shooting">avoided certain places because of it</a>. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07481187.2023.2214889">screening tools</a> to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.</p>

<p>Young adults have also grown up watching the same <a href="https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article313732975.html">heated gun debates</a> play out after every tragedy. <a href="https://www.everytown.org/issues/mass-shootings/">Gun control advocates</a> call for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.12857">stricter firearm restrictions</a> to prevent <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/the-looser-a-states-gun-laws-the-more-mass-shootings-it-has/">the next mass shooting</a>, whereas <a href="https://tpusa.com/live/mass-shootings-are-not-a-reason-for-gun-control/">gun rights advocates</a> push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase <a href="https://www.npr.org/2012/12/21/167824766/nra-only-thing-that-stops-a-bad-guy-with-a-gun-is-a-good-guy-with-a-gun">made popular by the National Rifle Association</a>. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses</a>. </p>

<p>Researchers have known for a long time that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00027162231164865">more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence</a>. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07418825.2020.1789693">2021 study</a> found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/390806181_NIJ_Final_Report_A_Comprehensive_Assessment_of_Deadly_Mass_Shootings_1980-2018">decades of mass shootings</a>, federal gun policy has <a href="https://www.bu.edu/articles/2022/the-long-failed-history-of-gun-control-legislation/">barely budged</a>. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including <a href="https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-statement-on-scotus-certification-in-challenge-to-connecticut-assault-weapon-ban">Connecticut</a> and <a href="https://www.jurist.org/news/2026/07/us-supreme-court-agrees-to-hear-challenges-to-assault-weapons-bans/">Cook County, Illinois</a>, they’ve faced <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-assault-weapons-debate-is-a-culture-debate-291639">Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court</a>.</p>

<p>Young people have become some of the <a href="https://time.com/7304031/march-for-our-lives-pam-bondi-shootings-jaclyn-corin/">loudest voices in this debate</a>, most notably through <a href="https://marchforourlives.org/">March for Our Lives</a> – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2018/06/28/texas-gun-control-high-school-student-activists-santa-fe-mass-shooting/">other youth-led groups</a> across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/07/24/key-facts-about-americans-and-guns/">older Americans</a>, many political observers assume <a href="https://iop.harvard.edu/press-releases/harvard-iop-youth-poll-finds-stricter-gun-laws-ban-assault-weapons-favored-two">stricter gun laws will follow</a> as young people <a href="https://now.tufts.edu/2026/09/22/young-voters-flex-their-power">gain voting power</a>.</p>

<p>This fall, voters in a few states will weigh in on gun policy directly.</p>

<p>In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_9,_Firearm_Regulations_Referendum_(2026)">keep or repeal a 2024 law</a> that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Arkansas_Issue_2,_Right_to_Keep_and_Bear_Arms_Amendment_(2026)">change the state constitution</a> to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.</p>

<h2>Young adults are split</h2>

<p>So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.70087">Our survey asked</a> young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.</p>

<p>In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.</p>

<p>We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high. </p>

<p>In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12340">largest voting bloc in the country</a>. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.</p>
