title: How to lose a job in five days
excerpt: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing at the White House on October 13, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appe
body: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing at the White House on October 13, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out of a job after only five days.  What happened? Zacharia was fired on Friday after less than a week in her new role, after a rocky start that included a halting performance in the briefing room, a scandal over her legal credentials, and a round of less-than-successful cleanup interviews .  The firing makes her the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in history, outstripping even first-term Trump communications director Anthony Scaramucci, who made it 10 or 11 days (figures vary) before getting the boot.  “Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci posted on Friday . “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.” (No word yet on whether the “Zacharia” will emerge as a unit of time, as the “Scaramucci” has.)  What’s the context? Zacharia’s remarkably short stint behind the podium unfolded as the White House is engaged in an unprecedented attack on press freedom: The administration is still trying to ban three media outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, though as of earlier this week, a judge is still blocking the ban from taking effect

The diminished nature of the press secretary job was on full display in Zacharia’s sole briefing on Tuesday , when she took questions from just three outlets: Breitbart, Fox News, and the Daily Mail.  Why does this matter? Zacharia’s no good, very bad week is not likely to leave much of a lasting mark in its own right — other than, perhaps, as pub trivia — but as NBC’s Garrett Haake points out , it’s a very tangible manifestation of a White House that seems to have no idea how to spin itself out of crisis with just weeks until the midterm elections.  Most recently, Trump has landed on flat-out lying about the state of the economy — but like Zacharia’s time as press secretary, it doesn’t seem like it’s going to go all that well

And with that, it’s time to log off… The underlying trend — municipal inaction — may be infuriating, but I loved this story about “tactical urbanism” from my colleague Sara Herschander.  As she writes, vigilante activists have taken to painting their own crosswalks, building benches, and even installing makeshift bike lanes in their neighborhoods — and every time they do, “they remind us that it is not actually that hard — or even that expensive — to do many of the simple things that can make our cities safer and more pleasant places to live.”  You can read Sara’s full piece here , no gift link needed
Enjoy, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

title: West Bank settlers brutally attack a Washington Post journalist
excerpt: Photojournalist Heidi Levine is transferred on a stretcher into an ambulance after she was attacked by Israeli settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers
body: Photojournalist Heidi Levine is transferred on a stretcher into an ambulance after she was attacked by Israeli settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers harvesting their olives on October 16, 2026. | Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
On Friday, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians living in the West Bank, as well as a Washington Post photographer, who was hospitalized with serious injuries
Photojournalist Heidi Levine was knocked down, beaten, and robbed of her camera equipment by masked settlers in an attack captured on video by other journalists
Those other members of the press rescued her from the attackers while Israel Defense Forces soldiers reportedly stood by
Levine had lacerations and a wound to her hand that split her finger to the bone, according to the Post , which condemned the attack in a statement
Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who helped Levine escape the attack, said that Levine also had cracked ribs, and may have been stabbed
Assaults like this one are becoming more common in the West Bank, where settler violence — which is currently targeting the ongoing olive harvest — has worsened

Last week, another photojournalist for the news wire Agence France-Presse was beaten with rifles by settlers, and Palestinian residents of the West Bank have been shot, beaten, and terrorized while the Israeli settlers targeting them face few consequences
Why settler violence is growing in the West Bank As my colleague Zack Beauchamp recently explained, under international law, the settler movement in the West Bank is clearly illegal
Nevertheless, it’s continued to grow, and it has a friend in the current Israeli government led by Benjamin Netanyahu

It’s also becoming increasingly violent.  Two current Israeli officials, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir, are settlers themselves, and both have used their offices — as ministers of finance and national security, respectively — to  further the settler cause , including by making it easier for settlers to commit unchecked violence against Palestinians.  The United Nations  reported in June that settler attacks had reached “the highest sustained levels ever recorded…with [an average of] six daily attacks that have resulted in casualties, property damage or both,” and in many Palestinians being forced from their homes by settlers

In late September , the International Committee of the Red Cross said that expanding Israeli settlements and violence by settlers was “making everyday life untenable” for Palestinian residents of the West Bank

As Zack has reported , settlements and settler violence are both intentional tactics, serving to force more Palestinians off their land, isolate the ones who stay, and push any potential two-state solution further out of reach.  That kind of violence is likely only to worsen in the weeks to come: Israel will hold elections on October 27, which could well result in Netanyahu’s settler-friendly government losing power
As a result, the Washington Post reported earlier this month , settlers are “racing to lock down gains” before the election with ever more extreme violence
One link for later ➨ Agentified kind of life
My colleague Adam Clark Estes turned the keys to his life over to a passel of AI agents for two weeks to see what would happen

They successfully saved him some times, he writes, largely with mundane tasks — but he left with mixed feelings about the experiment, including the possibility of contributing to a world with more AI slop

Before you go… Did you know… that the aerodynamic crouch used by jockeys in horse racing — known as the “martini glass position” — made race times roughly 5 to 7 percent faster ? Jockeys maintain it with only a few toes resting on each stirrup
Today’s trivia: Who is the author of the 1952 self-help book The Power of Positive Thinking ? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: We asked about the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything in  The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy
That would be the number 42 (take it up with Douglas Adams).

title: The case for data centers, explained by a person who wants you to like them
excerpt: The JPMorgan Chase data center in Orangeburg, New York, on October 14, 2026. | Kena Betancur/Getty Images Lately, AI data centers are public enemy No. 1
body: The JPMorgan Chase data center in Orangeburg, New York, on October 14, 2026. | Kena Betancur/Getty Images Lately, AI data centers are public enemy No. 1

The concerns are legion: how much water and electricity they consume, the noise they generate, the sprawling buildings they bring to communities, and the technology they’re powering that may or may not take all of our jobs and usher in the robot apocalypse
Earlier this year, Gallup found that 71 percent of Americans oppose building data centers that support AI in their communities
And the backlash is bipartisan: Majorities of Democrats, Republicans, and independents opposed local construction
Even in Texas, where data center development has been booming, Republican Gov
In September, he directed state regulators to halt permits for data centers pending audits examining their effects on the power grid and water resources
But while many data center projects have run aground, others are still getting built — and the companies behind them are employing experts like Nicole Thomas to smooth the way
Thomas is the senior vice president of media and community engagement at JSA, a marketing and public relations firm that represents data center companies
She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how the industry is responding to public opposition — and why she argues that these facilities can still be good neighbors
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  You’ve been at this for 21 years
Obviously, 21 years ago, data centers were not the hot-button issue they are today
When did you notice the shift? I’d say about two years ago
I came into this industry myself about four and a half years ago
I come from a state transportation background where community engagement is just paramount

When you’re putting a new traffic intersection up, they expect you to interact with the public.  When I got to this industry, I said, “Oh, what’s your community engagement like?” And they said, “We don’t even have any community engagements in this industry.” And they weren’t wrong
Because 21 years ago, [data centers] were just like infrastructure
It was like building a warehouse for your computers
And so it was very similar to the way that you would build a Costco
You would just go in, request a zoning permit, the zoning board would say, “Yeah, that works
Stamp, boom.” And you build your data center
And as a matter of fact, it was very secretive before, because data, and having that data in the wrong hands, has a lot of [cybersecurity] implications
About two years ago is when we started noticing the mainstream journalists coming around asking questions about data centers
It still feels secretive, I think, to a lot of people, and that’s why people are mad
If you read about this data center that was proposed in Utah by Mr
Wonderful, Kevin O’Leary , it caught a lot of people off guard
Seventy percent of Americans, at the moment, do not want them in their backyards
How do you go about trying to change that 70 percent’s minds?  First and foremost, I think education is really important
And so one of the things that we did notice very early on because of the previously secretive nature of data centers, there wasn’t a lot of education out there about what they even are
And so that’s something we need to change
We need to make the connection between [phones] and data centers so that people understand what a data center means to their life on a daily basis
Every app on your cellphone requires a data center to save your information in there
When you put your password into anything, you are interacting with a data center, which will verify your password and then let you into that app
Not to mention all of the information about you that you store in that app is then stored in a data center so that it can be recalled at any time
We could not be having this call without digital infrastructure
We can’t have email without digital infrastructure

And that stat about 70 percent of people not wanting the data center in their backyard — I’d be interested in seeing the stat of how many people actually live near a data center and don’t realize it.  Because there are nondescript data centers doing work quietly in your neighborhood that have been there for decades and you don’t even know it

And so in some ways I feel, and I think the industry does as a whole, but I won’t speak for them, that the pushback on data centers is somewhat related to the pushback on AI, because people can’t control AI
You even have Sam Altman telling us that AI will destroy society
So you have this concern about AI and you don’t know how to control it, but you can push back on data centers

title: Vermont once dreamed of universal healthcare. This Democrat wants to try again — with a twist.
excerpt: Protest signs seen at protect Medicaid lights up Capitol amid budget showdown, on May 7, 2025, in Washington, DC. | Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Caring Across G
body: Protest signs seen at protect Medicaid lights up Capitol amid budget showdown, on May 7, 2025, in Washington, DC. | Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Caring Across Generations Twelve years ago, Vermont Democrats tried to make their state the first in the nation to have a single-payer government-financed healthcare system — a bold experiment to push the limits of American health coverage when Obamacare was just being launched
Their plan failed , and rebooting it became politically impossible, even in Vermont: The Democrats lost the governorship to Republican Phil Scott for what turned out to be a decade
A progressive political newcomer named Amanda Janoo is taking on Scott in what polls show is a tight governor’s race

And if she wins, the state could be poised to try a whole new national experiment: one of Janoo’s central campaign promises is to create a pioneering health system where the state pays the full tab for primary and preventive care, while leaving the rest to the existing system

Key takeaways Amanda Janoo, the Democratic nominee for governor of Vermont, wants to move primary and preventive healthcare to a single-payer system — where the state would pay providers for such care, make it free for patients, and cut insurers out
Previous attempts to pass or enact full single-payer systems have failed at the state level, including in Vermont in 2014
Janoo is trying to focus first on this one relatively smaller slice of the health system, but hopes it could be a starting point to full single-payer reform eventually
Yet even this more limited reform faces difficult political and practical challenges
Janoo’s candidacy is an example of the policy experiments that are becoming possible nationwide in a projected “blue wave” year, when Democrats could sweep into power in a number of states
But in the healthcare universe, her plan is also an example of how even progressive policy idealists are trying to learn from past failures and focus on what they think can actually be achieved
Compared to the sweeping ambition of Vermont’s 2014 effort, or Bernie Sanders’s signature “Medicare-for-All” idea, Janoo’s proposal for single-payer has very specific limits

Under Janoo’s proposal for “universal primary and preventive care” (she typically avoids the term “single-payer”), the state government would pay for Vermonters seeing primary care providers such as doctors and nurse practitioners
This government coverage would be universal and free for patients, and insurance companies would be cut out
However, other parts of the health system – such as hospitals, specialists, and prescription drug companies – would remain under the existing insurance system, for now
Every effort so far to enact full single-payer at the state level has failed — even in blue states , bills and ballot initiatives have regularly gone down to defeat
Vermont’s previous single-payer experiment made it the furthest — it was signed into law but abandoned before being implemented, when the governor concluded it was unworkable
Wherever it’s gained steam, politicians and voters have blanched at the high costs of moving their health systems onto state budgets, and the high taxes that would be necessary to fund them

Now, Janoo is making an attempt to refurbish single-payer as something more achievable, by cutting off a smaller slice of it. “I think it’s clear at this point that a profit-oriented healthcare system is a terrible idea,” Janoo told me in an interview Monday
But after assessing that the state budget made it “unrealistic” to do single-payer immediately, she concluded, “we could do universal primary and preventive care,” financed by a tax on the wealthiest
Indeed, single-payer for primary care seems more achievable precisely because primary care is a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system

But Janoo hopes it will pay major dividends — that better preventive care will improve Vermonters’ health, reducing costs elsewhere in the system by, for instance, making some hospital visits unnecessary
In speaking to health policy experts about this idea, I heard much sympathy for the goal of universal primary care, but many questions about the details

Would Janoo’s plan be sufficient to bring more primary care doctors to Vermont — and, not unrelatedly, would it pay them more? Would her hoped-for cost savings from preventive care actually materialize? Is picking up the tab for a relatively less expensive part of the healthcare system the best use of sparse state funding? These questions are becoming national ones, as healthcare gains traction as a political issue again

It isn’t just Vermont where primary care reform ideas are gaining steam: Democrats in Minnesota , Washington state, and elsewhere have discussed them. “There is growing interest in a number of states across the country in doing a universal primary care for all program,” Kevin Grumbach, a family physician and a professor of family and community medicine at the University of California San Francisco, told me
Scott, Janoo’s opponent, signed a law calling for a study of universal primary care
One dividing line emerging, though, is whether to keep insurers involved, or to clear them out with a single-payer system, as Janoo wants
Insurers are unpopular with the public, but they can be a formidable political opponent when they argue that the benefits voters currently enjoy might be lost
Scott has said that the idea of universal primary care is appealing — but that if universal is “just code for single payer, I’m not interested

We’ve already been through that.” Yet Janoo is hoping that single-payer for primary care will be a stepping stone – a trial run for eventually making the rest of the state’s health system single-payer down the road. “I think about this often,” Janoo told me. “How do you build the new system as you transition the old — or hospice the old?” Amanda Janoo is tired of “corporate neoliberal bullshit” Janoo has long been an unorthodox economic policy thinker

Her rise is part of a broader trend in which progressives and leftists are winning primaries and gaining influence in the Democratic Party – but she doesn’t fit the prototype of the democratic socialist candidates in New York City , Colorado and elsewhere who’ve gotten much attention this year
Instead, she comes from a different strand of the left, a movement based on a dissident strain of economics and openly skeptical of the benefits of economic growth

Dating back to when she graduated from college in 2010, in the aftermath of the financial crisis, she was part of a younger cohort rebelling against what seemed the glaring failures of the economic establishment. “The one thing coming out of university I was clear on was that neoliberalism was the worst,” Janoo said on a podcast last year. “This whole idea that governments should just take a hands-off approach to the economy and trust in sort of the disciplinary powers of the global free market to lead them to infinite growth seemed highly problematic and very anti-democratic.” So for graduate school, Janoo attended Cambridge to study development economics under the “heterodox” economist Ha-Joon Chang
She then spent several years working abroad in international development for the United Nations and other organizations, before moving back to Vermont and working as an economic policy consultant

In recent years, Janoo became deeply involved with the “ well-being economy ” movement: an international group of advocates, academics, and experts who criticize what they deem modern capitalism’s obsession with economic growth, and say the “well-being” of humans and the environment should be prioritized instead

They overlap with the “ degrowth ” movement, which outright argues economic growth should be reduced; last year, Janoo led a workshop at a DeGrowth Institute event on “Degrowth Policy Design.” Trump’s return to power horrified Janoo. “I’m feeling angry about the rise of fascism and the growing threat of world war, because I feel like we don’t have time for this shit,” she said in a speech at an environmental event last year. ”The planet is on fire and ecosystems are collapsing, and that should really be the focus of all of our attention.” But, she said, “I believe I was born in this moment of history for a reason” and vowed “to fight for democracy – for life.” So Janoo decided to jump in the race for governor of Vermont

While she is not running on a degrowth platform, her campaign is deeply informed by aspects of the movement’s thought: skepticism about growth’s benefits, a sense that untrammeled capitalism is leading the world to disaster, and that localism provides a better way

For instance, candidates for governor typically pledge that they’d help bring business investment in, but Janoo said in a July debate : “A lot of the problems we’re facing is because we focus so much on attracting external business.”  “Our economy is not super-diversified, and it is not really centered in the most essential kinds of goods and services you want to make sure people have access to no matter what happens — because honestly, things are bad now and they’re going to get worse,” Janoo told me. “I feel a little bit like a collective prepper right now
My motto is, protect what we love, produce what we need.”  In the Democratic primary, Janoo’s opponent, Aly Richards, had closer ties to the party establishment and led in fundraising

But Janoo ran as a progressive outsider; she promised to advance a “more economically populist vision” instead of “corporate neoliberal bullshit.” Her health plan became a point of contrast with Richards, who said she wouldn’t run on “ magical thinking ,” and that she wanted a version of universal primary care that would keep insurance companies involved
Janoo won the primary by 2.5 percentage points

title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested

body: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report
Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status

body: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated

body: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law

body: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”
